[PATH:empirical] Natural experiments from platform API deprecations (e.g., Twitter/X API v1.1 shutdown in 2023, Facebook Graph API changes) — Analyzing the impact of these deprecations on dependent services (e.g., third-party clients, social media management tools) can reveal whether services that relied solely on the platform's API or authentication collapsed, while those with OAuth-based multi-provider authentication survived.

[PATH:empirical] Comparative case studies of identity provider diversification (e.g., migration from Facebook Login to Google Sign-In or Auth0) in small-to-medium web services — Tracking services that diversified their authentication stack before vs. after a hypothetical platform removal (simulated via policy changes or outages) can test the conditional claim: diversification should prevent collapse.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical modeling of platform-dependent ecosystems (e.g., network effects and single-homing vs. multi-homing in platform economics) — Formal models (e.g., from Rochet & Tirole, or Eisenmann et al.) can simulate the short-term collapse risk given API and authentication dependencies, and identify conditions under which diversification mitigates systemic failure.

scope.domain: platform dependency and API-based services, with emphasis on authentication lock-in

qualifier.condition: dependent services have not implemented OAuth-based multi-provider authentication

[PATH:empirical] Empirical studies of platform ecosystem dynamics: e.g., research on Amazon Marketplace removal or Facebook's acquisition history (e.g., Instagram, WhatsApp) and subsequent effects on niche app or e-commerce platform emergence. If removal triggers a wave of acquisitions or feature cloning by adjacent platforms, it supports the hypothesis; if independent niches flourish, it refutes it.
